Well friend, as someone who suffers from depression and has a long line of men with depression in my family, I feel you completely. I have had "episodes" where I would not get out of bed for a week. Two semesters ago I failed two classes because of attendance and to be honest, that year was one of the worst of my life due to personal issues involving family. Unfortunately, when you wallow and play video games, it is a form of escape in the same way eating junk food or drinking excessively is an escape. You don't want to deal with the issues there, so you delay them for that eight hours where you can play a binary game. If you are so depressed that you cannot even do that (I have been), then it is time to look toward baby steps. What do I mean by baby steps? Well, take the small victories and make a pact with yourself every morning that you will do one thing. I don't care what it is. For me, I would tell myself, "you just have to go outside and take a walk, just a 15-minute walk." So no matter what happened that day, no matter how bad I felt and wanted to be in bed, I took that walk. Yeah, maybe a walk doesn't seem like anything special, but it took me three days to do that walk after I made that goal. I came back home and I cried, and took a shower, and then cooked dinner for my partner. I did something. Maybe I didn't feel amazing yet, but I felt less bad. And firsthand, I saw that completing one goal, however small it was, made me complete something else I like doing. I love cooking dinner for my partner. I do it several times a week. That wasn't even my original goal. You have to take the small victories, man. Also, counseling. I am an advocate of therapists even when nothing is wrong. Life is stressful just by nature, and for depressed people, it is tenfold. For me, it was super difficult to talk to friends, family, or my partner about what I was feeling (I don't think even I knew) or what I wasn't feeling. Maybe I didn't want them to worry about me, or see me as weak, or whatever it was. Talking to a counselor is a no-strings-attached engagement. What I mean is that this person does not pluck the strings of your life or puppeteer anything that affects your life or relationships. They listen and speak to you about your issues. They are not friends; they are there to serve your emotional well-being. I think counseling and therapy is one of the most important things ever. By far. It feels amazing to drain some of the pent-up feelings (sometimes they make sense after you have let them out). You can cry in front of these people and share your scary thoughts or doubts with them. Then you can go back home and focus on those little victories. It takes time, man, and I deal with it every day. You have to be accountable for your own feelings. Good luck. The issue is that nowadays the people making horror movies are not good directors in general. A legendary filmmaker was an incredible director who could have probably done any genre, but chose horror. Jump scares are an element of horror, but not the only thing in the movie. Modern horror popcorn flicks want people to enjoy the theater experience, so jump scares take precedence over the core necessities of any movie including story, structure, character, finer details, etc. They all follow the same formula which is exposition in which something that "doesn't feel right" happens or is happening like a family moving into a new house and the dog doesn't want to go in, or a locked basement door, or a shot held on a character we haven't introduced yet. And then that is the extent of the story, character, structure, all those things I said. Now, the scares happen, but the issue is that we only jump because in a theater the sound is so loud and the screen is big in a dark room. Your body actually flinches, not because of the horror, but because of the sudden-ness. We do not care about the characters because the exposition felt like something on a checklist. So you have flat characters in peril or conflict and there is no tension. Why do I care if main character A lives? He was developed for a few minutes and we don't even know who he is or who she is. Or any of them. The reason that movies like a classic horror film, or even further back, another classic, are so scary is because the characters are developed and placed in a structured story that our brain can logically work through. We are not robots, yet writers in the industry think that. The main girl in one of those classic films dies early on, yet we understood her in a way and it was terrifying to watch her get killed. Then the private investigator, and her sister and husband are all developed as well. The scenes in between modern jump scares are literally there just so the scares are not one right after the other. Often involves the main character doing something basic like folding clothes or taking a child to school or whatever. Like really develop the characters - make them do something that gives us information about them. Even though a recent film is not strictly horror, I think it employs many elements that are necessary in horror. The characters are all following an arc. There is character payoff, which makes us like these characters. A specific example is when one character is telling another about how he got into a state university and was going to leave the town. He bought his bus ticket, then ended up not leaving and he has regretted it since. Spoilers. Then after he is killed, the main character finds his bus ticket on his person/wallet. The payoff is tangible. You feel sorrow and maybe hatred for the killing of that character not only because he did not accomplish that thing, but also because the main character's new friendship came to an end in tragedy. This whole effect creates a scare - towards another character. You did not need a jump scare to do that. You just needed a setup and payoff that was organic to the characters such as a young guy getting into university and not leaving his small town, then finding the ticket in his wallet showing that he kept that regret on him literally.
